extracted.intended_audience: aspiring writers and prospective public contributors (general readership considering publication)
extracted.subtask_description: Prescriptive guidance on when a person ought to write or publish: criteria for subject-matter competence, stylistic mastery, preparation, and the acceptable exceptions for unlettered discoverers. Focused on judging readiness to instruct the public and avoiding harmful or useless publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper qualification to write (must impart something necessary)
rubrics_metrics.description: He who has not obtained the proper qualifications of an author can have no excuse for the arrogance of writing, but the power of imparting to mankind something necessary to be known.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only the possession of something genuinely necessary or useful to communicate excuses publication without formal learning. An uneducated person may on occasion reveal a useful thought or intelligence that merits divulgence, but such cases are rare; most publications merely transpose common sentiments. Writers should therefore examine whether they truly have useful information before publishing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perfect knowledge of the subject
rubrics_metrics.description: The first qualification of a writer is a perfect knowledge of the subject which he undertakes to treat; since we cannot teach what we do not know, nor can properly undertake to instruct others while we are ourselves in want of instruction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To justify claiming knowledge a writer should have read and compared the writers who have previously discussed the topic, familiarized their arguments by long meditation, consulted the foundations of different systems, and separated truth from error by rigorous examination. Without this preparation, the writer wastes both his time and his readers' and exposes himself to derision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mastery of language and appropriateness of style to purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: He must be master of the language in which he delivers his sentiments: if he treats of science and demonstration, that he has attained a style clear, pure, nervous, and expressive; if his topicks be probable and persuasory, that he be able to recommend them by the superaddition of elegance and imagery, to display the colours of varied diction, and pour forth the musick of modulated periods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match style to subject: technical/scientific writing requires clarity and precision; persuasive or rhetorical writing benefits from elegance, imagery, varied diction and rhythmic periods. Mastery of language is a distinct prerequisite from subject-knowledge; you must be able to express thoughts with perspicuity and elegance to instruct or persuade effectively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence of readiness through study of models and habitual practice
rubrics_metrics.description: He only can rationally presume that he understands a subject, who has read and compared the writers that have hitherto discussed it... In like manner, he only has a right to suppose that he can express his thoughts with perspicuity or elegance, who has carefully perused the best authors, accurately noted their diversities of style, diligently selected the best modes of diction, and familiarized them by long habits of attentive practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Read the best models, note stylistic differences, select and internalize effective diction and structures, and practice over a long period. Both intellectual readiness and stylistic competence are demonstrated by sustained study and habitual imitation/experiment; they are not achieved by chance or vanity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid publishing without study or formed style (anti-pattern)
rubrics_metrics.description: He that without forming his style by the study of the best models hastens to obtrude his compositions on the publick, may be certain... he shall shock the learned ear with barbarisms, and contribute, wherever his work shall be received, to the depravation of taste and the corruption of language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rush to publish. Premature publication leads to linguistic barbarisms and harms public taste. The writer should delay submission until style has been formed through study and practice; otherwise the work is likely to be ridiculed and harmful to literary standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contribution must add real knowledge or usefulness (avoid mere repetition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Of the innumerable books and pamphlets that have overflowed the nation, scarce one has made any addition to real knowledge, or contained more than a transposition of common sentiments, and a repetition of common phrases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim to add something substantive—new facts, insights, or useful communication—rather than repeating commonplaces or merely rewording familiar ideas. The standard for publication should be contribution to knowledge or useful instruction; otherwise abstain from publishing for reputation alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contributions to periodicals and unsolicited assistance should be substantial and relevant
rubrics_metrics.description: Among these are the innumerable correspondents of publick papers, who are always offering assistance which no man will receive, and suggesting hints that are never taken; and who complain loudly of the perverseness and arrogance of authors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When writing letters, notes, or short submissions to newspapers/journals, ensure the material is of sufficient substance and relevance to be accepted. Habitually offering unsolicited, unusable assistance or hints is pointless and often ignored; good contributions anticipate usefulness to editors and readers rather than seeking attention.
